newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG prime minister calls for release of army chief.
newsitem.headline: PNG prime minister calls for release of army chief.

text.p: Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Bill Skate on Monday ordered soldiers to release the country's defence chief from house arrest and called for charges against troops involved in an army revolt in March to be withheld.

Skate said he could not meet the soldiers' demand for a general amnesty for troops involved in the March revolt, which resulted in two days of looting, mass protests, and the expulsion of 70 African mercenaries brought in to quell a separate rebellion on the island of Bougainville.

However, Skate said he had directed the police commissioner and attorney general to "withhold all charges" pending a new inquiry into the US$36 million mercenary deal with British military consultant Sandline International.
Papua New Guinea soldiers on Monday placed the defence chief Brigadier Colonel Leo Nuia under house arrest, defence spokesman Colonel Jack Tuat told Reuters, but he gave no further details.

A small group of soldiers had earlier overpowered police to free from jail Major Walter Enuma, who led the operation to expel the African mercenaries. Enuma was due in court on Monday to face firearm charges related to the recent June election.

"The prime minister has directed the release of the commander ...," Skate said in a statement. "He also directed that all operations currently undertaken by the commander and the special force unit cease immediately."

Three carloads of soldiers overpowered police to free Enuma from Port Moresby police cells overnight after visiting the major on the pretext of bringing him clothes, Australian Broadcasting Corporation radio reported.
Local media have reported that the commander of the March revolt, former Brigadier General Jerry Singirok, will be charged with sedition on his return to Papua New Guinea on Tuesday.
Following talks between Skate, a senior army officer and the soldiers' lawyer, the prime minister agreed to re-open the Sandline inquiry and order all charges be held in abeyance.

Skate said he now "pleaded for calm and understanding and for the release of the commander and the other senior officer who are currently being held under house arrest". The identity of the other senior officer was not immediately clear.

"The prime minister has therefore appealed for the members of the defence force to give his government a chance to be fully briefed on the Sandline crisis and for the inquiry to be completed before the government can make clear and considered decisions in relation to those people involved," Skate said.

In March, Papua New Guinea was rocked by its worst crisis since independence in 1975, when the army revolted against the hiring of mercenaries to end a nine-year secessionist revolt on Bougainville island.
The revolt sparked two days of looting and mass protests in the capital Port Moresby which forced the then prime minister Sir Julius Chan to step down.

A judicial inquiry into the mercenary deal cleared Chan of any wrongdoing and he returned to office within weeks of the election. But a voter backlash against political corruption and the mercenary deal saw more than 50 politicians, including Chan, lose their seats.
A new government, which included the former ruling coalition parties, was formed last week, headed by prime minister Skate, who campaigned against the mercenary deal and corruption.
